video.title: Read before you write: PRIMM and tracing
video.format_note: Animated explainer, 16:9, flat Darsi colours on paper-grey backgrounds. Code is typed out on a card, left to right in both languages. Narration in the lesson language; captions as separate files, never burned in.
cast: Dr Farah — education lecturer, Bangladesh (main character)
Mr Joseph — computer studies teacher, Kenya (cameo)
Narrator — the Darsi voice (warm, peer to peer)

scenes.narration: Write a program to add up these marks, I said, and the whole class froze. Nobody had ever read a program, so nobody knew where to start. Children read many stories before they write one; code is the same.
Today: PRIMM, and tracing a program line by line.
PRIMM is a way to plan a programming lesson, from researchers in England. Its five stages are Predict, Run, Investigate, Modify and Make. Pupils read and predict before they write anything.
Start with a short program that works. Pupils predict, in writing, what it will print. Then you run it. A wrong prediction isn’t a failure: it shows exactly what a pupil believes about code.
To check a prediction, trace the program. A trace table has a column for each variable and a row for each line that runs. Pupils fill it in on paper, exactly as the computer would.

Then go deeper. Investigate with questions: what does line two do, what if x were ten? Modify: change one thing and predict again. Only at the end, Make: a new program of their own, using the same idea.
Quick check! x is five, y equals x, then x becomes seven. What does print y show?
Five. Many pupils say seven, because they think y is linked to x for ever. That’s a misconception, and a trace table shows it at once: line three changes x, but y’s column stays at five.

Why does reading first work? Writing from a blank screen asks a beginner to do everything at once. Reading and tracing build a picture of what each line does. In a study in English secondary schools, pupils taught with PRIMM did better in a programming test.
PRIMM needs very few devices. Predict and Investigate happen on paper. Run is one phone, held up or passed round. Pupils only need their own device for Modify and Make, and pairs can share.

scenes.on_screen_text: App lab: step through a program
scenes.narration: In the app, open Step through a program and choose if and else. Fill in a trace table on paper first, then press Next and check each row against the variables.
Your turn. In a PRIMM lesson, what do pupils do before they run the program?

They predict. Remember: PRIMM is Predict, Run, Investigate, Modify, Make. A wrong prediction shows what a pupil believes. A trace table follows every variable, line by line. And most of it needs only paper.

Try it in class tomorrow: a PRIMM starter. Show a four-line program, and have pupils write their prediction before anyone runs it. Then run it, and ask those who were wrong to explain their thinking first.

checkpoints.prompt: x = 5, y = x, then x = 7. What does print(y) show?
checkpoints.feedback_correct: Correct — y got a copy of 5. Changing x later doesn’t change y.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite — y = x copies the value 5 into y. When x changes, y stays 5.

checkpoints.prompt: In a PRIMM lesson, what do pupils do before running the program?
checkpoints.feedback_correct: Correct — Predict comes first, then Run, Investigate, Modify and Make.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite — the P in PRIMM is Predict: pupils commit to a prediction before running.
